name: journal-what-paul-never-said-about-jesus.json
content:
Thirteen of the New Testament's twenty-seven books carry Paul's name, and he says almost nothing about what ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (ʿalayhi al-salām, peace be upon him) taught. I mean the seven letters scholars accept as his: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. In them I find no parable, no healing, no sermon on a mountain and no prayer taught to disciples. The omissions are the point of this post.

He does know some facts. ʿĪsā was "born of woman, born under the law",1 "descended from David according to the flesh",2 and had a brother, because Paul met "James the Lord's brother".3 He knows the supper, the crucifixion and the resurrection. What he does not give is a life. In those letters he never names Nazareth, Galilee, Bethlehem or Mary, and he tells the Corinthians the reason: "I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified".4

[paulus_figure name="sea-of-galilee-shore-wooden-boat-emp-5192542"]Wooden boats on the Sea of Galilee. Paul never mentions Galilee, where the gospels place most of the teaching of ʿĪsā.[/paulus_figure]

The sayings he does cite can be counted on one hand. On divorce: "To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband".5 On pay: "the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel".6 On the supper: "This cup is the new covenant in my blood".7 To the Thessalonians he gives "a word from the Lord" about those who have died.8

Luke adds one more, and it is the strangest. In Acts Paul tells the elders at Ephesus to "remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'"9 Paul himself never writes it down.

Paul also draws a line between the Lord's teaching and his own opinion, and he draws it twice in one chapter. "To the rest I say (I, not the Lord)",10 and later "I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment".11 The honesty is plain. It also shows that when the Lord had said nothing, Paul went on teaching.

[paulus_figure name="mustard-plant-seeds-18346906"]A heap of small seeds. ʿĪsā likened the kingdom of heaven to a grain of mustard seed (Matthew 13:31); Paul never repeats the parable.[/paulus_figure]

Set that beside what is missing. The prayer is in [paulus_link slug="the-prayer-jesus-taught" /]. The first commandment, the Shema, and the words "why do you call me good?" are in [paulus_link slug="jesus-in-his-own-words" /]. Paul has one echo of how ʿĪsā prayed, "Abba! Father!",12 and he has no parable or healing story to put beside it.

The famous verse people raise is "Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer".13 Read either way, it matches his practice. Paul never met the teacher in his life on earth ([paulus_link slug="did-paul-ever-meet-jesus" /]), and he says he took his gospel from no man ([paulus_link slug="a-self-appointed-apostle" /]).

[paulus_figure name="wildflowers-lilies-field-10903308"]Orange lilies in a garden. "Consider the lilies of the field" is a saying of ʿĪsā (Matthew 6:28) that Paul never repeats.[/paulus_figure]

The Qurʾān keeps the other half. It records what ʿĪsā told his people: "O Children of Israel, worship Allāh, my Lord and your Lord."14 That is the centre of his message: the worship of God alone. [paulus_link slug="the-injil-and-the-letters" /] sets the Injīl of the Qurʾān beside the letters.

So the gap is the case in small. The letters carry the cross and the resurrection and almost nothing of the man who taught, and the church that formed around them built on what they carried.

What Paul never said of ʿĪsā: questions readers ask

Did Paul quote Jesus?

Rarely. In the seven letters accepted as his, the clearest cases are on divorce (1 Corinthians 7:10), pay for preachers (9:14), the supper (11:23–25) and the dead in Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:15).

Did Paul know the gospels?

The letters never cite one. Most scholars date Mark, the earliest gospel, after all seven of the letters accepted as Paul's, so he could not have used it for them.

What did Paul say about the life of Jesus?

That he was born of a woman under the law, descended from David, had a brother James, held a last supper, was crucified, buried and raised. He gives no place of birth, no miracle and no parable.

Why does it matter what Paul left out?

Because the teaching of ʿĪsā, what he asked of those who heard him, is missing from the letters that define Christian belief. The cross carries the weight in Paul where the teaching carries it in the gospels.
